You are synthesizing technical specifications from 3 AI models for "Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts" in the context of Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing.

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts (0A)
Accepted scope: Remote survey (observing programme and survey data) plus electric-propulsion rendezvous scouts with subsurface sampling and bulk assay. Replaces the monopropellant prospector fleet.

- T18 Subsurface sampling and in-situ bulk grade assay: TRL 2–4 now, target 8, AD² 6, project-ending

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-2 Mining Robots; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

## Model Specifications:

## Claude Opus 5.5

# bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts: Technical Proposal (Phase 0A, gated 0B option)

**Basis.** 2026 USD. Costs come from analogy and engineering judgement unless a calculation is shown.

**Scope.** This proposal addresses the accepted scope: a remote survey (observing programme and survey data) plus electric-propulsion (EP) rendezvous scouts with subsurface sampling and bulk assay. It replaces the monopropellant prospector fleet.

**Provenance.** The round-2 reconciliation describes a 12–16 × ~200 kg remote-sensing fleet. That predates the binding re-scope to 4–10 scouts of 200–600 kg with subsurface sampling. I treat the reconciliation's sizing as superseded and use its analyses only where they still apply.

---

## 0. Bottom line

| Parameter | Recommendation | Range | Basis / confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Remote survey | Observing programme plus data analysis. **No dedicated telescopes.** | 1 programme, 2027–2038 | Existing assets cover the pre-screen. Medium confidence. |
| Scouts | **6** (2 pathfinder tranche + 4 gated) | 4–8 in 0A; 0–2 optional in 0B | Binomial sizing on pre-screen hit rate p = 0.3–0.5 (§7). Low–medium confidence. |
| Scout wet mass (iodine reference) | **550 kg** | 460–600 kg | Bottom-up budget, 15 % system margin (§4.3). Medium confidence. |
| Scout wet mass (argon alternate) | 610 kg | 560–660 kg | Breaches the 600 kg envelope unless one Surface Assay Package (SAP) is deleted or Δv is cut. Medium confidence. |
| Design Δv (EP) | **4.5 km/s** from C3 ≈ 0 | 3.5–5.5 km/s | 1 full plus 1 secondary rendezvous. Low confidence until the accessibility study is done. |
| Array power, BOL at 1 AU | **3.6 kW** | 3.0–4.5 kW | 2.5 kW to EP plus 0.4–0.7 kW bus |
| Surface Assay Packages per scout | **2** (each hops to 2–3 sites) | 1–2 | Up to 6 cored sites per scout |
| Sampling depth | **1.0 m** | 0.5–1.5 m | Mining robots work the top ~1 m. Rationale in §5.2. |
| bom-0-1 cost, 0A | **$680M** | $495–900M | Survey + development + 6 flight units + data products (§13). Low–medium confidence. |
| bom-0-1 cost, 0B option | $0–150M | – | 0–2 site-confirmation scouts plus survey continuation |
| All-in mission cost incl. other lines | ~$0.95B before reserve | $0.66–1.28B | Adds launch, DSN, ops and spares from bom-0-8/9/10/14 |

My position on the round-2 figures:
- I agree with Claude's quantity of 6 (range 4–8).
- I disagree with every round-2 unit cost as too low for a craft that carries a subsurface sampler. My figure is about $100M per scout fully amortised and $50–75M recurring.
- I reject Gemini's two telescopes outright.

---

## 1. Design philosophy

### 1.1 What decision this item exists to support

bom-0-1 serves one decision: the **Target gate** (one of the four D-02 discriminating gates) before KDP-0B. It does not exist to discover asteroids, catalogue taxonomy, or do science.

The question at that gate is whether at least one named NEA has:
- a **recoverable** Fe-Ni grade,
- regolith mechanics,
- spin state, and
- tug accessibility

that together let bom-0-2, bom-0-3 and bom-0-4 close at 0.6–2.5 kt/yr, with stated confidence, plus one backup.

Every instrument, kilogram and dollar below is justified against that question.

### 1.2 Why remote data alone cannot answer it (the null option)

I evaluated the null option: external data only, no scouts. **I reject it.** Remote data can tell us "S-type, radar-bright, about 15 % metal by meteorite analogy." It cannot tell us the four things the plant and robots depend on:

1. **Recoverable metal fraction and liberation.** How much metal reports to a magnetic concentrate after comminution, and at what grain size. This governs the processing plant's mass balance and is invisible remotely.
2. **Sulphur and phosphorus deportment.** Troilite (FeS) intergrown with metal sets the refining burden.
3. **Regolith depth, cohesion and grain-size distribution, top 1 m.** OSIRIS-REx is the cautionary datum: OVIRS identified phyllosilicates correctly, but nobody predicted the near-zero cohesion. The TAG head sank ~0.5 m.
4. **Spatial variability.** Grade at the 10–100 m scale over the area actually mined.

The value-of-information case is straightforward. bom-0-1 costs about $0.7–1.0B. 0B commits multiple billions in irreversible hardware to one rock. Cutting false-commit probability by even 10–20 percentage points pays for this item.

### 1.3 Opinionated principles

1. **Ground truth, not breadth.** Breadth is already bought by the world: SPHEREx, NEO Surveyor, Rubin, Gaia and IRTF. We pay for depth.
2. **Measure what the plant measures.** The core assay is a miniature beneficiation test: sieve, magnetic separation, weigh, then XRF the concentrate. A spectrum that must be converted to grade through a meteorite model is not enough.
3. **Put sampling risk on a cheap expendable, not the propulsion bus.** The mothership never touches down. SAPs land, anchor, core, assay and hop.
4. **Gate by evidence, not by calendar.** I adopt GPT's evidence-based gates. Tranche 2 is sized after tranche 1 has actually cored.
5. **Do not let scouts drive the propellant decision (D-05).** Fleet propellant is under 1 t against hundreds of tonnes for the tugs. Scouts can, however, be the first in-space data point for kW-class iodine Hall operation. That is useful to bom-0-4, so I exploit it with a fallback.
6. **Data-buy compatible.** Every scout requirement is written as a data-delivery requirement as well as a hardware requirement. That lets a commercial provider bid fixed-price "delivered assay per target."

### 2.1 Target funnel

| Funnel stage | Count | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Known NEAs | ~38,000 (growing ~3,000/yr with Rubin) | MPC |
| Size D ≈ 0.3–3 km and spin period P > 2.2 h | ~5,000–8,000 | NEO Surveyor diameters/albedos; Rubin and ground lightcurves |
| Scout-accessible (≤ 3.5 km/s low-thrust from C3 ≈ 0) **and** tug round trip to SEL1 within the bom-0-4 budget | ~150–600 | RSP accessibility study |

| Commit-grade | **≥ 2 required** (1 primary + 1 backup) | Target gate |

The size floor is set by regolith retention, not by tonnage. A 200 m body holds about 8 Mt, centuries of supply at 1 kt/yr of metal. Bodies under ~300 m, or spinning faster than ~2.2 h, tend to be bare or monolithic, which defeats tethered regolith mining. Numbers marked ~ are my estimates pending the RSP accessibility study.

## 3. Element A: Remote Survey Programme (RSP)

### 3.1 Content

| Work package | Content | 0A cost (range) |
|---|---|---|
| A1 Catalogue ingestion and fusion | Pipelines for SPHEREx (0.75–5.0 µm, 102 bands, all-sky), NEO Surveyor (4–5.2 and 6–10 µm, from ~2028), Rubin colours/lightcurves, Gaia DR3 reflectance spectra (~60k asteroids). Bayesian taxonomy and metal-likelihood model. | $4–8M |
| A2 Purchased ground spectroscopy | IRTF/SpeX 0.7–2.5 µm and LXD 3 µm on shortlist passes. Time on other 3–10 m facilities via partnerships or purchase. ~30–60 objects. | $6–15M |
| A3 Planetary radar campaigns | Goldstone DSS-14, GBT bistatic and any new facility: radar albedo (metal discriminator), shape, spin. Limited to close passes (≲ 0.05–0.1 AU), so opportunistic: ~10–20 objects. | $5–12M |
| A4 Low-thrust accessibility study | Optimised low-thrust scout transfers (1- and 2-target chains), plus round-trip tug accessibility to SEL1 jointly with bom-0-4. Launch-window maps 2030–2040. | $2–5M |
| A5 Pre-screen hit-rate validation | Retrospective test of the pre-screen model against Itokawa, Ryugu, Bennu, Eros, Didymos/Dimorphos and Psyche (2029). Meteorite-fall orbit linkages. Produces the prior on p. | $1–3M |
| A6 Meteorite-analog laboratory | 100–200 kg of H, L, LL and E chondrite bulk material (NWA material, roughly $1–10/g in bulk) for assay calibration and processing feedstock tests. Shared with bom-0-3 and bom-0-11. | $2–4M |
| A7 Analysis team | 5–8 FTE × 11 yr | $10–20M |
| **Total RSP, 0A** | | **$30–67M; nominal $45M** |
| RSP 0B continuation | Monitoring, backup-site watch, Phase 1 feed | $5–15M |

### 3.2 Disagreement: no dedicated telescopes

Gemini's two telescopes would cost $45–120M each, as applied in round 2. I reject them for three reasons:
1. The binding constraint is ground truth, not discovery or taxonomy.
2. SPHEREx has already flown the 3 µm survey capability a smallsat telescope would provide, at a better aperture-time product than we could afford.
3. Any telescope aperture we could fund is beaten per dollar by purchased IRTF and radar time.

If SPHEREx asteroid extraction under-performs (open question Q3), the fallback is purchased IRTF/LXD time, not a spacecraft.

I set RSP at $30–67M. That is inside Claude's $20–60M at the upper end, and GPT's $100M ceiling is unnecessary without hardware.

### 3.3 RSP deliverables (exit criteria)
- **By scout PDR (2028):** ranked shortlist ≥ 15 objects, each with VNIR class, diameter/albedo, spin period and low-thrust Δv for 2030–2034 windows.
- **By tranche-2 CDR (2032):** shortlist ≥ 25, including ≥ 8 with radar or SPHEREx 3 µm data. The pre-screen p prior is updated with tranche-1 results.
- **Continuously:** target dossiers for bom-0-4 trajectory work.

## 4. Element B: Scout mothership

### 4.1 Top-level requirements (draft, verifiable)

### 4.2 Δv budget (iodine reference, Isp ≈ 1,700 s)

| Leg | Δv (km/s) | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| C3 ≈ 0 → primary rendezvous | 3.0 (2.2–3.5) | Low-thrust equivalent of NHATS-class 1.8–2.8 km/s impulsive, plus ~15–25 % gravity/steering loss |
| Primary → secondary (60 % of scouts) | 1.2 (0.6–1.5) | Requires an A4 chain search. Many pairs exceed this, which is why only ~60 % of scouts get a secondary. |

Comparison with round 2:
- Gemini's 3.2 km/s with 65 kg is internally inconsistent: 65 kg at 2,100 s on ~210 kg implies about 7.6 km/s.
- Claude's 5.0 km/s assumed two full rendezvous on a 200 kg craft.

My 4.5 km/s reflects a more expensive primary than Claude assumed, because the target must also be tug-accessible, plus a cheaper, opportunistic secondary.

**Argon alternate (D-05).** Argon stored supercritical at 300 bar is about 0.48 g/cm³, giving ~260 L for ~125 kg. A COPV for that volume weighs about 28–35 kg, against ~8 kg for the iodine tank. Argon Hall efficiency at kW class is about 30–40 % versus about 45–50 % for iodine, which needs ~10 % more array or longer thrust time. Net result: **+45 to +70 kg, wet ~610 kg, breaching the 600 kg envelope.** Recovering the envelope with argon means one of:
- one SAP per scout,
- Δv cut to ~3.8 km/s (no secondary targets), or
- accepting ~650 kg and revisiting the launch packing (bom-0-8).

**Low-confidence item.** Dry mass for this class historically grows 20–35 % from PDR to launch. That growth would consume the secondary-target capability first, so I declare the secondary target a descope lever, not a requirement.

### 4.4 Power and thrust performance

- **EP operating point:** 2 × 1.25 kW at ~300 V. Iodine Hall: η ≈ 0.45, Isp ≈ 1,700 s. Per thruster, T ≈ 2ηP/vₑ ≈ 67 mN, so the system gives ~135 mN.
- **Acceleration:** at 550 kg, 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ m/s². For 4.5 km/s at a 0.85 duty cycle, with a power derate to ~0.75 at 1.25 AU, total thrusting is about 0.8–1.1 yr.
- **Throughput per thruster:** ~62 kg, about 4,300 h at ~4.0 mg/s. **Qualification life test: 1.5× → ~6,500 h, or ~95 kg iodine.** This is the single longest-pole test in the item (§12).
- **Bus loads:** cruise ~400 W. Proximity peak ~700 W (payload, transponder, heaters, iodine-feed heaters off). SAP relay ~30 W.

### 4.5 GNC and proximity operations
- **Optical navigation.** Approach uses star-referenced centroiding. Proximity uses landmark/natural-feature tracking (OSIRIS-REx NFT and Hayabusa2 heritage), fused with lidar ranging.
- **Proximity profile.** Hover/terminator orbits at 1–5 km, with a gravity-assisted shape model built in-flight. Dips to 100 m for SAP release.
- **Abort logic.** The descent abort decision is made on board (§8). The mothership never descends below 50 m.

### 5.2 Sampling approach and why

I traded five approaches:

1. **Touch-and-go on the mothership** (OSIRIS-REx style): top ~5 cm only, one shot, and it puts the propulsion bus at risk. **Rejected.**
2. **Kinetic impactor** (Hayabusa2 SCI): exposes ~1 m strata, but the material is then remote-sensed, not assayed. It also produces large ejecta, which conflicts with bom-0-15. **Rejected as baseline.**
3. **Penetrator:** gives mechanics but recovers no sample to assay. **Rejected.**
4. **Pneumatic sampler** (PlanetVac-type, flown on the Moon in 2025): excellent in loose regolith. It needs gas, and its depth is limited to ~10–30 cm. **Retained as a secondary/backup head** for shallow grab samples if the drill stalls.
5. **Anchored lander with rotary-percussive drill to 1 m: BASELINE.**
   - It matches the mining robots' working depth.
   - It gives a stratigraphic profile.
   - Its contact forces and power draw are themselves geotechnical data for bom-0-2.

**Anchoring is the critical risk.** Philae's harpoons failed, and the lander bounced. Mitigations:
- Low-reaction screw anchors (3 legs).
- Cold-gas hold-down thrust during drilling (~0.5 N, short bursts).
- A drill reaction-torque limit that keeps stall torque below anchor capacity.
- Weight on bit of ≤ 5 N.

The drill needs to reach only 1 m. It must handle cohesionless granular material up to centimetre clasts. If it meets a boulder or monolith, it relocates by hopping.

### 5.3 Assay cell: "beneficiation in a box"

Process per core interval (four intervals per core: 0–10, 10–30, 30–60, 60–100 cm; 20–60 g each):

1. **Centrifuge-assisted sieving** at 0.5–1 g artificial gravity. Size fractions: < 0.1, 0.1–0.5, 0.5–2, > 2 mm. This gives the grain-size distribution.
2. **Crush** the > 2 mm fraction to < 1 mm (mini jaw/roll). This gives a liberation proxy.
3. **Magnetic separation** with a permanent-magnet drum (~0.3 T) in the centrifuge. Products: magnetic and non-magnetic fractions.
4. **Mass measurement** of each fraction with a resonant/inertial balance (works in microgravity), target ±2 % of fraction mass.
5. **Micro-XRF** on each fraction: Fe, Ni, Co, S, P, Si, Mg, Ca, Cr. This yields Ni/Co in metal, and S in concentrate (troilite carry-over).
6. **NIR microscope** (MicrOmega-class) for silicate mineralogy and hydrated phases.
7. **Evolved-gas analysis.** Stepped heating to 1,000 °C with a quadrupole mass spectrometer: H₂O, CO₂, SO₂/H₂S, organics. This is essential for C-types (bom-0-6) and for S.
8. **Contact gamma/neutron spectrometer** (CeBr₃ + He-3-free neutron detector, ~3 kg). It integrates 3–7 days per site for bulk Fe/Ni/H over ~0.3–0.5 m depth. This is the bulk check against the core-scale assay. **Option to delete** at PDR if the mass budget fails.

**Primary output:** *recoverable metal fraction (wt %) of run-of-mine regolith after < 1 mm comminution and single-pass magnetic separation, with concentrate composition*. This is the number bom-0-3 needs.

## 7. Fleet sizing and tranching

### 7.1 Requirement

**P(≥ 2 commit-grade Fe-Ni targets) ≥ 0.85**: one primary plus one backup.

A C-type for bom-0-6 is **opportunistic, not sized for**. bom-0-6 is conditional on a C-type target, and forcing one into the fleet would add ~2 scouts for a pilot that may never proceed.

### 7.2 Model

Characterised targets n = N × s × k, where:
- s = 0.8 is scout survival through the primary campaign (first-of-kind deep-space EP smallsat class; my judgement),
- k = 1.6 is targets per surviving scout (1 + 0.6 secondary),
- p is the probability that a pre-screened shortlist target proves commit-grade.

| p (pre-screen hit rate) | n for P(≥ 2) ≥ 0.85 | Scouts N |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 6 (P = 0.89) | **4–5** |
| 0.4 | 8 (P = 0.89); 7 gives 0.84 | **6** |
| 0.3 | 10 (P = 0.85) | **8** |

**Caveats.** Hits are not independent. We visit best candidates first (which helps), and the pre-screen model may share systematic errors (which hurts). The A5 validation and tranche-1 results are the only defences. That is why the fleet is tranched.

### 7.3 Tranches

## 10. Contamination, debris and planetary protection (inputs to bom-0-15, D-03)

- **Planetary protection:** NEA targets are COSPAR Cat I–II. There is no sample return.
- **Assay integrity:**
  - Green-monoprop exhaust contains H₂O, CO₂ and N₂, which would corrupt hydration and C measurements. Rules: cold gas only below 500 m; witness plates on each SAP; full exhaust log.
  - Main EP plume (iodine deposition on optics and arrays, and on the surface) is excluded within 20 km during campaigns.
- **Ejecta:** escape speed at a 500 m body is ~0.2–0.3 m/s. Drilling, hopping and landing can loft material above it.
  - **Proposed interim ceiling for this item:** ≤ 100 g per site liberated above escape speed; no particles > 1 cm intentionally lofted.
  - The final number belongs to bom-0-15 under ALARP.
- **End of life:** scouts either remain as sentinels and are then disposed to a heliocentric orbit with no close approach to the target or SEL1 within 100 yr, or make a controlled landing outside the designated mining area. The choice is made with bom-0-15.

Representative splitting, grain-size effects, sample loss, and preparation bias are therefore part of T18—not ancillary laboratory details.

---

## 8. Resource evidence and downstream interfaces

### 8.1 Scout data are not automatically an ore reserve

Four stations and eight increments can still miss large-scale heterogeneity.

Every resource package must distinguish:

1. Direct measurements.
2. Spatial extrapolations.
3. Process-model predictions.
4. Unresolved uncertainties.

If the observed variability prevents a credible lower-bound estimate, the result is **“insufficient evidence”**, not a forced grade declaration.

### 8.2 Target acceptance package

Deliver to bom-0-2, bom-0-3, and programme gate authorities:

- Shape model, spin state, gravity estimate, and their uncertainties.
- Surface-unit and hazard maps.
- Local contact mechanics and anchoring results.
- Sample locations, depths, handling histories, and losses.
- Elemental composition and phase fractions.
- Grain-size distribution and coarse-metal observations.
- Magnetic-separation response.
- Estimated accessible inventory with explicit confidence bounds.
- Radiation, thermal, lighting, and communications environments.
- Delivery trajectories evaluated against the current Phase 1 destination.
- Unresolved failure modes and recommended follow-up.

### 8.3 Grade must close against the process model

An illustrative—not approved—screen might require:

- Native/reduced Fe-Ni fraction: 20 wt%.
- Recoverability into accepted intermediate product: 70%.
- Subsequent product yield: 90%.

Then overall product yield is:

\[
Y=0.20\times0.70\times0.90=0.126
\]

Delivering 1,000 t/yr would require approximately:

\[
\dot m_{\rm feed}=\frac{1{,}000}{0.126}\approx7{,}940\ {\rm t/yr}
\]

The appropriate threshold depends on the actual plant, accessible inventory, transport losses, signed demand, and permitted operating duration.

The scout does **not** certify recoverability from composition alone. Process recovery must be supported by validated ground correlations and the separate relevant-environment processing demonstration.

### 8.4 Phase 1 demand interface

Before KDP-0B, Phase 1 must supply a controlled specification covering:

- Annual and cumulative tonnage.
- Delivery dates and destination.
- Permitted Fe/Ni composition range.
- Oxygen, sulfur, carbon, phosphorus, and other relevant impurity limits.
- Physical form and dimensional tolerances.
- Receiving inspection and rejection criteria.

Scout target rankings must be rerun when this specification changes.

---

## 9. Autonomy, navigation, and communications

### 9.1 Autonomy requirements

Earth round-trip light time is approximately **17 minutes at 1 AU separation** and **50 minutes at 3 AU**. Ground control cannot manage terminal contact in real time.

Use testable requirements rather than an undefined autonomy “level.”

The spacecraft shall autonomously:

- Maintain a safe proximity trajectory through a communications outage.
- Detect disagreement between optical navigation, ranging, and predicted motion.
- Abort a descent before violating a certified stopping-distance envelope.
- Detect excessive contact force, slip, drill stall, or anchor loss.
- Stop and retract a sampling tool without ground intervention.
- Reject assays that fail standards or contamination checks.
- Enter a power-positive, thermally safe state after a single credible fault.
- Preserve a minimum evidence dataset through recorder faults.

Ground approval remains mandatory before:

- First close approach.
- First contact.
- Sampling a materially different terrain class.
- Starting a second-target departure.
- Actions with significant contamination or trajectory consequences.

### 9.2 Navigation

Baseline sensors:

- Star trackers and inertial sensors.
- Wide- and narrow-angle optical navigation.
- Laser rangefinder for terminal operations.
- Radiometric Earth tracking.

A dedicated navigation beacon for mining robots is **not baseline**. The scout may provide a time-limited local reference service only if reliability and remaining lifetime justify it; industrial operations must not depend on a scout surviving indefinitely.

### 9.3 Communications architecture

Reference:

- X-band uplink/downlink.
- 20 W RF transmitter.
- 0.6–0.8 m high-gain antenna.
- Low/medium-gain coverage for safe mode.
- Modern error correction, packet prioritization, and disruption-tolerant file delivery.

Planning downlink:

- **Approximately 1–50 kb/s**, depending on range, geometry, receiving aperture, coding, and weather.
- Use **10 kb/s effective delivered rate** for preliminary data-volume planning.
- Do not assume free DSN access.

A 0.6 m antenna at X-band has approximately 32 dBi gain. With a 20 W transmitter and a capable 34 m-class receiving station, a 10 kb/s-class link at roughly 2 AU is plausible, but requires a formal link budget and contracted receiving performance.

### 9.4 Data volume and ground time

Commit to **2–5 GB of prioritized science data per primary target**, with much larger raw datasets retained onboard.

At 10 kb/s:

\[
t(1\ {\rm GB})\approx222\ {\rm hours}
\]

Thus 2–5 GB requires approximately **444–1,111 hours**, before additional navigation and operational overhead.

Plan for:

- Approximately **600–1,450 antenna-hours per target** for this delivered dataset.
- Approximately **2,000–4,500 antenna-hours/year fleet peak allocation**, depending on overlap and actual link rates.
- Explicit station handover, solar-conjunction, and outage allowances.

Compress images and select spectral cubes onboard, but retain calibration, uncertainty, and provenance information. Do not downlink only an algorithm’s final classification.

---

## 10. Manufacturing and verification

### 10.1 Manufacturing approach

Use a common bus with a configuration-controlled payload module.

Recommended practices:

- Common electrical and mechanical interfaces across all scouts.
- Identical flight computers, radios, power electronics, and primary navigation hardware where practical.
- Qualified commercial components where radiation and reliability analysis support them.
- Lot-controlled critical parts.
- Replaceable assay cartridges and sample-path assemblies before launch.
- Witness coupons and contamination monitors near sample handling and propulsion interfaces.
- Strict material compatibility controls for iodine.
- Continued supplier access to test fixtures and failure-analysis support.

Avoid creating a second spacecraft variant for speculative flyby tours.

### 10.2 Verification priorities

The essential facilities are:

1. Thermal-vacuum EP performance and endurance testing.
2. Abrasive sampling and sample-preparation testing.
3. Gravity-offloaded contact-dynamics rigs.
4. Reduced-gravity tests for acquisition, splitting, retention, and transfer.
5. Hardware-in-the-loop optical navigation and autonomous abort tests.
6. Integrated thermal-vacuum campaigns with flight-like assay hardware.
7. End-to-end data exercises from raw measurement to resource decision.

Ground rigs cannot perfectly reproduce small-body dynamics. Their limitations must remain explicit in TRL assessments.

### 10.3 Reference sample library

Develop a blinded validation library spanning:

- Native Fe-Ni grains in silicate matrices.
- Coarse metal inclusions.
- Metal-rich and oxide-rich assemblages with similar magnetic responses.
- Altered surfaces over different subsurface material.
- Weak rubble and cohesive fines.
- Multiple particle-size distributions.
- Plausible contamination and sample-preparation artifacts.

Score the assay system on its ability to distinguish economically important alternatives, not merely to reproduce a favorable simulant.

---

## 11. Development roadmap and readiness gates

The supplied panel envelope places T11 and T18 at **TRL 2–4**, with **AD² approximately 5–6 and 6**, respectively. Heritage components do not automatically raise the integrated sampling scout to flight readiness.

### 11.1 Indicative schedule

Dates below assume effective authorization around late 2026/2027. They are planning ranges, not committed launch opportunities.

| Period | Main work and exit evidence |
|---|---|
| 2027–2028 | Purchased survey begins; target catalogue; assay breadboards; anchor and sampler trades |
| 2028–2029 | Integrated sampling/assay engineering model; reduced-gravity tests; preliminary optimized transfers |
| 2029–2031 | Flight design, propulsion qualification, integrated verification, first-pair acceptance |
| Approximately 2031–2033 | First-pair launches, subject to target windows and readiness |
| Launch + 1–3 years | First rendezvous campaigns |
| First campaigns + 0.5–1.5 years | Sampling, assay, interpretation, and follow-up decisions |
| Thereafter | Further pairs, process pathfinder, and possible KDP-0B |

A late-2030s industrial decision may be realistic if substantial redesign or additional target campaigns are required. Do not sell a fixed three-to-five-year industrial gate as a pass criterion.

### 11.2 Gates

**Gate A—Survey and architecture**

Require:

- A viable shortlist with optimized low-thrust transfers.
- Sufficient observing evidence to justify flight expenditure.
- Initial T11/T18 breadboards at TRL 4–5.
- Explicit decision criteria and a target-yield uncertainty model.

**Gate B—First-pair flight commitment**

Require:

- Closed mass, power, thermal, link, and transfer budgets.
- Relevant-environment subsystem evidence adequate for the approved flight risk.
- Representative autonomous-contact and assay demonstrations.
- Contracted launch/injection and ground-network access.
- Propellant downselect supported by life and supply evidence.

**Gate C—Additional scout pairs**

Require:

- Updated target yield and common-cause reliability assessment.
- Evidence that another pair has greater decision value than redesign, alternative sourcing, or stopping.
- Incorporation of first-pair lessons where available.

**KDP-0B—Industrial commitment**

Apply D-02 without waiver:

- Every project-ending technology at **TRL 6 in a relevant environment**.
- Target, demand, economics, and licence gates all passed.
- Processing behavior demonstrated through the appropriate separate pathfinder.
- Representative sampling and assay uncertainty low enough to support the proposed industrial commitment.

The scout programme should ultimately target **TRL 8** after qualification and successful operational demonstration, but TRL 8 is not a substitute for the four programme gates.

---

## 12. Cost estimate and procurement strategy

### 12.1 Direct bom-0-1 estimate

**Basis:** Six roughly 500 kg spacecraft carrying substantial sample-acquisition and assay payloads.

| Direct element | Quantity/basis | Cost |
|---|---|---:|
| Survey data and observing programme | One multi-year programme | $20–60M |
| First scout pair, recurring flight hardware and acceptance | $55–85M each | $110–170M |
| Subsequent four scouts | $40–65M each | $160–260M |
| **Direct bom-0-1 total** | **Six scouts** | **$290–490M** |

The first-pair premium covers low-rate production, extensive recurring calibration, and less mature manufacturing. Common design development and qualification remain in bom-0-11.

### 12.2 Quantity sensitivity

| Fleet | Direct bom-0-1 estimate |
|---:|---:|
| Four scouts | $210–360M |
| Six scouts | $290–490M |
| Eight scouts | $370–620M |
| Ten scouts | $450–750M |

The programme should contract options rather than create an unconditional obligation to purchase ten.

### 12.3 Attributable lifecycle view

These amounts belong to the indicated BOM owners and **must not be added again inside bom-0-1**.

| Cost element | Owner | Six-scout allowance |
|---|---|---:|
| Direct survey and scout hardware | bom-0-1 | $290–490M |
| Common NRE, assay development, qualification | bom-0-11 | $150–300M |
| Launch and injection | bom-0-8 | $80–200M |
| Allocated ground-network services | bom-0-9 | $40–90M |
| Flight operations | bom-0-10 | $80–160M |
| Allocated spares | bom-0-14 | $20–40M |
| Allocated contamination assurance | bom-0-15 | $10–25M |
| EP supply and qualified batches | bom-0-16 | $2–8M |
| **Subtotal before reserve** | | **$672–1,313M** |
| Provisional reserve, approximately 25–35% | bom-0-17 | **$168–460M** |
| **Attributable lifecycle envelope** | | **Approximately $0.85–1.8B** |

Reserve is a provisional planning allowance pending a quantified cost-risk analysis. The upper bound is not a statistical P80 claim.

Excluded:

- Unallocated bom-0-7 programme overhead.
- The separate processing/mining pathfinder.
- Industrial assets and receiving-node construction.
- Inflation, financing costs, and taxes not yet specified.

### 12.4 Phase allocation

- **0A:** All currently proposed survey and scout expenditure.
- **0B:** No automatic recurring allocation. Retasking surviving scouts may be inexpensive, but additional scouts, monitoring requirements, and replacement missions require a separately approved scope.

### 12.5 Where I disagree with round 2

1. **Approximately 200 kg is too aggressive for the accepted scope.**  
   It may suit a remote-sensing rendezvous mission, but subsurface acquisition, restraint, sample preparation, and defensible bulk assay materially change the spacecraft.

2. **$12–35M recurring hardware is not my baseline.**  
   It lacks sufficient allowance for the sampling and assay scope. Approximately **$40–85M per flight unit**, depending on production stage, is more credible for planning.

3. **Do not procure dedicated telescopes initially.**  
   Purchased observing capacity is more reversible. Reconsider a telescope only after documenting a specific information gap and lifecycle advantage.

4. **Do not baseline multiple rendezvous per scout.**  
   Propellant capability alone does not establish a feasible sequence or useful arrival date.

5. **Do not average the historical fleet proposals.**  
   The revised industrial architecture needs a smaller, evidence-driven target set, not the target pool implied by abandoned plant and robot quantities.

6. **Do not inherit conflicting heritage cost citations.**  
   None of the contradictory MarCO figures is used to normalize this estimate. Obtain verified mission cost scopes and supplier quotations.

---

## 13. Principal risks and mitigations

| Risk | Consequence | Mitigation / stop criterion |
|---|---|---|
| Spectrally promising targets lack usable native metal | No industrial target | Early multimodal screening; retain stop option; update target priors |
| Sampling system cannot react forces or retain material | T18 failure | Competing acquisition breadboards; force-controlled restraint; reduced-gravity testing |
| Samples are spatially or granulometrically biased | False industrial commitment | Stratified sampling; coarse-fraction accounting; duplicate splits; explicit uncertainty gate |
| XRF/XRD cannot reliably distinguish relevant metal forms | Grade overstated | Blinded reference library; reject unvalidated matrices; no magnetic-only certification |
| Iodine EP life or contamination performance fails | Delay/redesign | Early endurance test; argon alternate; isolate sample path |
| Low-thrust transfer takes too long | Evidence arrives after demand window | Optimize full trajectories before commitment; fund orbit refinement and backup targets |
| Common software or mechanism fault affects all scouts | Fleet-wide loss | Independent verification, staggered launches, paired procurement, fault injection |
| Communications capacity unavailable | Incomplete evidence | Contract network capacity before launch; prioritized data products |
| Dust or ejecta escapes | Contamination, licence breach | Enclosed acquisition, capture and retention, quantified release assessment |
| Target licensing or authorization fails | Mission cannot proceed | Early legal engagement; documented activities and disposal plan |
| Representative microgravity metallurgy fails | 0B does not close | Keep 0B gated; use Earth-supplied material fallback rather than force commitment |

### Debris and contamination requirement

Apply ALARP under interim D-03, with a **modelled interim ceiling approved by the licensing authority**. Do not invent a universal acceptable release fraction.

Design requirements should include:

- No intentional uncontained impactors in the baseline.
- Captured drill cuttings and retained assay residues.
- Quantified particulate release by size, velocity, and destination.
- Predicted plume deposition at sampled surfaces.
- Tool and mechanism fragment retention.
- Passivation and target-specific end-of-mission trajectory assessment.
- A prohibition on disposal that creates an unacceptable future Earth-encounter risk.

A “99% capture” statement is not an adequate safety case.

---

## 14. Open engineering questions

The following should be resolved before freezing the flight design:

1. **Target availability:** How many candidates actually close the power-constrained transfer and industrial-delivery problem in the intended windows?
2. **Target requirement:** Is one qualified site sufficient, or must a fully characterized backup exist before 0B?
3. **Required grade confidence:** What false-commit probability is acceptable for the planned industrial expenditure?
4. **Sample representativeness:** Can approximately 1–2 kg acquired across four stations support the required inference, particularly for coarse metal?
5. **Anchoring envelope:** Can one restraint system cover the likely surface classes, or should the first pair deliberately carry different acquisition heads?
6. **Assay discrimination:** Can the compact preparation/XRF/XRD chain achieve its targets on high-metal, coarse-grained samples?
7. **Propulsion:** Which iodine or argon implementation closes lifetime, contamination, thermal, efficiency, and supply requirements?
8. **Trajectory delivery:** Which injection services can provide the required departure geometry, rather than merely a cheap LEO or GTO rideshare?
9. **Ground network:** What effective data rate and antenna time can be purchased at the actual mission ranges?
10. **Processing correlation:** Which scout measurements most strongly predict plant recovery, impurity rejection, and product acceptance?
11. **Licensing:** What sampling, release, proximity, and disposal constraints will the authorizing state impose?
12. **Null option:** At what updated cost and target-yield estimate should Project Dyson stop prospecting and adopt Earth-supplied material?

---

## 15. Recommended authorization

Approve the following initial package:

- **One purchased observing and survey-data programme.**
- **Two flight scouts**, designed within a 400–600 kg envelope.
- Options for **two additional pairs**, with an outer planning limit of ten scouts.
- A dedicated T18 sampling-and-assay maturation effort under bom-0-11.
- Early procurement studies for launch injection and paid deep-space communications.
- Configuration-controlled interfaces to mining, processing, contamination control, and Phase 1 demand.

Name a technical authority under bom-0-7 and issue a controlled baseline identifying assumptions, cost ownership, document versions, and superseded legacy requirements.

**Bottom line:** Build a small fleet capable of discovering that an asteroid is unsuitable—and of proving suitability when the evidence supports it. The programme succeeds by enabling a defensible industrial decision, including a decision not to proceed.

---

# bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts: Consensus Synthesis (Phase 0A, gated 0B option)

**Basis.** 2026 USD. The three inputs are Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-6.1 Sol. Where Gemini's current proposal departs from its own round-2 figures, the current proposal is used.

---

## Key Specifications

These points are common to all three models.

- **Two-tier architecture with no dedicated telescopes in the initial buy.**
  - Pre-screening comes from purchased or external observations: ground spectroscopy, radar and existing space surveys such as NEO Surveyor.
  - Dedicated scouts then follow up a shortlist.
  - Gemini's current proposal drops the two round-2 telescopes in favour of a $20M grant-based screening line.
  - Survey-programme allowances span $20M (Gemini) to $20–60M (GPT) to $30–67M (Claude).

- **Every scout is a rendezvous mission; no flybys.**
  - Each scout has one primary target.
  - A secondary target is opportunistic and is not a baseline requirement.
  - GPT does not credit it. Gemini allows it "only via extended mission geometry". Claude makes it the first descope lever, although his fleet-sizing model still credits 0.6 secondaries per scout.

- **Solar-electric Hall propulsion, with iodine as the reference case (consistent with D-05).**
  - Launch is to C3 ≈ 0.
  - Ideal EP Δv capability is 3.5–4.8 km/s: Gemini 3.5, Claude 4.5 design (3.5–5.5), GPT 4.81 ideal with ≤3.5 allocated to the primary transfer.
  - Isp is 1,700–2,200 s.
  - The iodine feed system (heated, corrosion-controlled) and thruster life testing are the long-pole propulsion risks.

- **Remote data alone cannot support the Target gate.**
  - All three require physical ground truth at the asteroid before mining robots or industrial assets are committed.
  - The quantities that must be measured in place are regolith cohesion and mechanics, grain size, and metal form and abundance.

- **Common remote-sensing core on the scout:**
  - VNIR/SWIR spectrometer reaching about 3.4–3.8 µm, for hydration context;
  - 8–14 µm thermal-IR imager or radiometer, for thermal inertia and grain size;
  - narrow- and wide-angle optical navigation cameras;
  - low-contamination cold-gas control for fine proximity work. The main EP is not fired near the surface.

- **Gated, tranched procurement.**
  - A first pathfinder tranche flies and returns data before the remaining scouts are committed.
  - The size of later tranches is set by tranche-1 results.
  - Building the full fleet is not automatic.

- **Onboard autonomy is mandatory.**
  - Round-trip light time is about 17–50 minutes.
  - Autonomous optical navigation, hazard avoidance, safe-hold and descent-abort logic are therefore required.
  - DSN time is not free. The fleet needs thousands of procured antenna-hours per year at peak: Gemini ~4,000; GPT 2,000–4,500; Claude 5,000–9,000.

- **Data return and life.**
  - X- or Ka-band downlink at roughly 10–60 kbps at operational ranges, with a 0.5–0.8 m high-gain antenna.
  - Several GB of prioritised data per target (2–10 GB). Round-1 figures of tens to hundreds of GB are rejected.
  - Primary life 4–5 yr; extended goal 7 yr.
  - Battery 1–2 kWh.

---

## Divergent Views

- **Fleet size and spacecraft class**:
  - Claude recommends 6 scouts (range 4–8), each about 550 kg wet (460–600 kg), carrying two Surface Assay Packages.
  - Gemini prefers 12 scouts of 250 kg wet (205 kg dry), on a 1.5 kW, 600 W single-thruster bus.
  - GPT suggests 6 scouts as a planning reference (envelope 4–10), each about 500 kg wet (400–600 kg) on a 4 kW array.
  - Fleet sizing also differs. Claude sizes for P(≥2 commit-grade targets) ≥ 0.85. Gemini assumes a 25 % hit rate yielding 3 sites. GPT's illustrative model shows six scouts give only about 58 % probability of ≥2 qualifying targets, so six cannot be claimed sufficient if a backup is mandatory.

- **Subsurface sampling method (scope compliance)**:
  - Claude recommends expendable anchored landers. Two SAPs per scout, each about 42 kg, use screw anchors and a rotary-percussive drill to 1.0 m, followed by an in-situ "beneficiation in a box": sieve, crush, magnetic separation, microgravity mass balance, micro-XRF, EGA and contact GRNS. The mothership never descends below 50 m.
  - Gemini prefers a 2 kg spring-loaded kinetic impactor observed from hover, with no sample acquisition or bulk assay.
  - GPT suggests an articulated 1.5–2 m sampling arm on the scout itself, with restraint downselected after testing. It specifies ≥0.3 m minimum and 1 m goal penetration, 8 or more increments across 4 stations, and an XRF + XRD + magnetic-separation chain. It explicitly rejects uncontained impactors.

- **Cost level and accounting boundary**:
  - Claude recommends $680M nominal ($495–900M) for bom-0-1 0A. This includes $240M of item-specific development and implies about $100M all-in per scout ($55–70M recurring), plus a 35–50 % reserve.
  - Gemini prefers $569M, which includes launch ($90M) and ops/ground ($85M) that belong to bom-0-8/9/10. Its recurring cost is $22M per unit.
  - GPT suggests $290–490M direct, covering survey plus recurring units at $40–85M each, with $150–300M of NRE placed in bom-0-11. Its lifecycle envelope is $0.85–1.8B including reserve.

- **Pathfinder tranche size and gating**:
  - Claude recommends 2 pathfinders, then 2–6 more at a "Gate A". Gate A requires a core to ≥0.8 m and assay within ±15 %. Tranche-2 long-lead items are ordered at T1 CDR + 12 months.
  - Gemini prefers 4 pathfinders followed by 8 production units, on a compressed schedule: launch at year 2.5, gate at year 4.
  - GPT suggests three gated pairs. Each later pair is justified only if it beats redesign, alternative sourcing or stopping.

- **Propulsion rationale and alternate**:
  - Claude recommends iodine with argon as the D-05 alternate. He quantifies that argon adds 45–70 kg and breaches the 600 kg envelope unless one SAP or the secondary target is dropped.
  - Gemini prefers iodine chosen deliberately as a tug-commonality pathfinder, with krypton as the fallback. Krypton is not the D-05 alternate.
  - GPT suggests selecting neither propellant yet and not forcing scout–tug commonality. It sets a qualification target of 12,000–16,000 equivalent hours, against Claude's 6,500 h.

- **Bulk-composition and contamination details**:
  - Claude recommends contact gamma/neutron spectroscopy on the SAP, with no orbital GRNS. He keeps a 20 km main-EP exclusion zone and sets an interim limit of ≤100 g per site lofted above escape speed.
  - Gemini prefers no GRNS. It uses an autonomy-"levels" framework and does not address an ejecta limit.
  - GPT suggests no GRNS baseline. It adds XRD and a magnetometer, uses a 1 km EP exclusion as a planning value, and requires captured cuttings, deferring any release ceiling to licensing under ALARP.

---

## Open Questions

1. **Joint accessibility.** How many metal-plausible NEAs are reachable by a 3.5 km/s low-thrust scout *and* support tug round trips to SEL1 (D-04) in 2030–2040 windows? Claude's falsifier: fewer than 20 such candidates would reopen the target strategy with bom-0-4.

2. **Anchoring and sample representativeness in micro-g.**
   - Can a drill with ≤5 N weight-on-bit, or an arm with positive restraint, reach 0.3–1 m in cohesionless regolith with cm-scale clasts without exceeding anchor capacity? Philae is the cautionary case.
   - Can about 1–2 kg from 3–4 stations bound grade heterogeneity and the coarse-metal "nugget effect"?
   - Should the first pair deliberately fly different acquisition heads?

3. **Assay validity against the process model.**
   - What recoverable-metal threshold closes the bom-0-3 mass balance at 0.6–2.5 kt/yr? Claude's placeholder is ≥8 wt % (5–15). GPT's illustration of 20 % metal × 70 % recovery × 90 % yield implies about 7.9 kt/yr of feed per kt of product.
   - Can a compact magnetic-separation + XRF/XRD chain distinguish native Fe-Ni from magnetite and replicate full-scale beneficiation to within about ±10 %?

4. **Propellant closure.**
   - Does 1–2 kW iodine Hall operation reach ≥3,000 h by PDR with acceptable erosion and plume deposition?
   - If not, does argon close the mass, efficiency and tankage budget inside 600 kg?

5. **Decision thresholds and ground capacity.**
   - What false-commit probability will the programme authority accept? This in turn decides whether a fully characterised backup site is mandatory, which drives fleet size between 4 and 10.
   - Can bom-0-9 procure 4,000–9,000 deep-space antenna-hours per year for 2033–2038, and at what cost?

6. **Instrument margins.**
   - Can an uncooled microbolometer reach the SNR needed for thermal-inertia mapping without a cryocooler (Gemini)?
   - Does contact GRNS add enough bulk-grade value over direct sampling to earn its about 3 kg (Claude versus GPT)?

---

## Recommended Approach

1. **Adopt a 6-scout reference fleet within a 4–8 unit authorisation, procured as an initial pair plus evidence-gated follow-on tranches.**
   - Each scout is about 500–550 kg wet within the 400–600 kg envelope, with a 3.6–4 kW BOL array and about 2–2.5 kW to EP.
   - Each carries one credited primary target. Secondary targets are uncredited upside.
   - Reject Gemini's 12 × 250 kg impactor configuration. It does not deliver the accepted scope of subsurface sampling and bulk assay, and its uncontained impactor conflicts with bom-0-15.
   - Size later tranches from the posterior hit rate after the first pair cores.
   - If programme policy requires a characterised backup site, plan toward the upper end (8 units).

2. **Carry two competing T18 sampling architectures to PDR, then downselect on reduced-gravity and vacuum test evidence.**
   - Option A: Claude's anchored, hopping SAP landers drilling to 1 m. This keeps contact risk off the propulsion bus.
   - Option B: GPT's articulated arm with force-controlled restraint.
   - Requirements for both: ≥0.3 m demonstrated penetration (1 m goal) and ≥6–8 cored increments across ≥3 geologic units.
   - Keep a pneumatic shallow head as backup.
   - Fund this as the item's top technical priority, since T18 is AD² 6 and project-ending.

3. **Specify the assay as a measured recoverability test, not a spectral inference.**
   - Combine Claude's process chain (sieve, crush, magnetic separation, microgravity mass balance, micro-XRF, EGA) with GPT's XRD phase discrimination.
   - Calibrate against a blinded meteorite and simulant library that includes magnetite-bearing decoys and coarse-metal samples.
   - Primary deliverable: recoverable Fe-Ni wt % with concentrate Ni, S and P and explicit uncertainty. "Insufficient evidence" is a permitted outcome.
   - Set the commit-grade threshold from the bom-0-3 mass balance and the Phase 1 material specification, not inside this item.

4. **Fund the purchased remote survey and accessibility study immediately, with no dedicated telescopes; budget $30–60M for 0A.**
   - Ingest external catalogues; buy IRTF/3 µm spectroscopy and radar time.
   - Run a joint scout/tug low-thrust accessibility study with bom-0-4 by PDR.
   - Retrospectively validate the pre-screen hit rate against visited asteroids.
   - Deliver a shortlist of ≥15 candidates by PDR and ≥25 by the second-tranche decision.

5. **Follow D-05 literally on propulsion.**
   - Cost iodine as the reference and argon as the alternate. Do not substitute krypton (Gemini) or treat tug commonality as a selection driver.
   - Start the iodine wear test now: ≥3,000 h by PDR, then a qualification life of ≥1.5× mission throughput. That is about 6,500 h on Claude's profile; GPT's 12,000–16,000 h is the conservative bound.
   - Pre-declare the argon mass response: one SAP per scout, or no secondary target.
   - Fleet propellant is under 1 t, so it should not drive the programme-wide propellant decision.

6. **Fix the cost boundary, then budget against it.**
   - Item-specific scout, sampler and assay development sits in bom-0-1. Cross-cutting test facilities sit in bom-0-11. Launch, ground, ops, spares and propellant stay in bom-0-8/9/10/14/16.
